newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria students keep up protests, truce unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria students keep up protests, truce unlikely.

text.p: Bulgarian students wearing red blindfolds marched past the ruling Socialist Party headquarters on Saturday to back opposition calls for early elections as the the two sides remained far apart on forming a new cabinet.

"We want a future in Bulgaria now", "We want a new parliament free of communists," said signs carried by two students with a blindfold on one eye as they led a dozen other students completely blindfolded through the streets.
Around 2,000 students joined the march and thousands more opposition demonstrators held a rally outside the gold-domed Alexander Nevsky cathedral to demand elections.

Despite 19 days of opposition street protests and the threat of more serious unrest to come, the Socialists still insist that they should form a new government to replace that of Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21.

The constitution requires President Petar Stoyanov, who took office on Wednesday, to ask the Socialists as the biggest party in parliament to form a government, but the opposition has threatened mass protests and a general strike if he does so.
"First we need to prevent formation of a second Socialist cabinet," the leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), Ivan Kostov, told the rally.

Both the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), composed largely of communists, and the opposition showed no signs of compromise on Friday at a first round of talks mediated by Stoyanov, who was elected on the opposition ticket.

"The week the mandate (to form a government) is handed out must be the week of our wrath," UDF deputy leader Filip Dimitrov, a former prime minister, told protesters as they chanted "Elections" and "Red trash out."
The UDF will hold a party convention in mid-February to discuss election campaign strategy and the policies aimed at hauling Bulgaria out of its crisis, UDF officials said.
Economists said last week Bulgaria's economy had plunged into hyper-inlfation for the first time as the monthly inflation rate for January was expected to hit 50 percent.
The central bank warned politicians that it alone could not contain the crisis and lifted administrative controls on interest rates from Monday, which economists say will boost inflation.
Shops have closed down as shopkeepers fear to stock up with goods whose prices change within hours, while impoverished consumers are buying only basic foods.

Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate a new accord with the International Monetary Fund, which has suspended disbursements because the Socialist government failed to implement the last reform programme.

The national currency, the lev, dipped to new lows of 920-930 to the dollar on expectations of further political instability and the central the bank fixed the currency at 813.87 for Monday, down on Friday's 731.71.
